record.paper_title: High Open-Circuit Voltages in Lead-Halide Perovskite Solar Cells – Experiment, Theory and Open Questions
record.original_question: Why do interfaces between perovskite absorbers and organic electron and hole contact layers exhibit extremely low surface recombination velocities despite the expectation that high-energy vibrational modes in organic semiconductors could make recombination faster, and what fundamental model of interface recombination would enable rational interface design rather than trial-and-error contact selection?

evidence.quote: In addition, the models for recombination generally only describe bulk recombination but not interface recombination. At an interface, defects are more likely to form than in the bulk. Therefore for most inorganic solar cell materials, interface recombination is even more important than bulk recombination.

This concept applied to interfaces between perovskite absorbers and organic electron and hole contact layers would suggest that organic interface materials might accelerate recombination because it is easier to dissipate the energy into the organic material. However, this doesn’t seem to be the case, given that perovskite/organic interfaces have extremely low surface recombination velocities [35,62,96]. Thus, a better fundamental understanding of interface recombination is needed to design interfaces rather than find suitable ones by trial and error.

artifact.category_tag: interface recombination in perovskite solar cells
artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a heterojunction in a thin-film solar cell formed between a lead-halide perovskite absorber (e.g., CH3NH3PbI3 or a mixed-cation, mixed-halide analogue) and an adjacent organic charge-transport layer used as either an electron contact (such as PCBM or C60) or a hole contact (such as Spiro-OMeTAD or PTAA). Let S denote the effective interface (surface) recombination velocity governing nonradiative carrier loss at this interface, defined operationally through the boundary condition J_rec = q·S·Δn for excess minority-carrier density Δn at the interface.

Standard nonradiative recombination theory (e.g., multiphonon emission and Marcus–Jortner-type models) predicts that the rate of nonradiative band-to-band or trap-assisted recombination should increase when high-frequency vibrational modes are available to accept the released electronic energy. Organic semiconductors possess high-energy intramolecular vibrational modes (C–H, C–C, C=C stretches at energies on the order of 100–400 meV), which by this reasoning ought to enhance nonradiative recombination at perovskite/organic interfaces compared to perovskite/inorganic interfaces.

Empirically, however, perovskite/organic interfaces are observed to display extremely low effective surface recombination velocities (often comparable to or lower than perovskite/inorganic counterparts).

Problem: Construct a quantitative, predictive microscopic model of nonradiative interface recombination at perovskite/organic-semiconductor heterojunctions that
(i) explains the observed smallness of the effective surface recombination velocity S despite the presence of high-energy vibrational acceptor modes in the organic layer;
(ii) identifies the dominant physical parameters controlling S (e.g., interfacial electronic coupling, energy-level offsets, reorganization energies, vibrational mode spectrum, dielectric screening, density and energetics of interfacial defects); and
(iii) yields design rules that allow rational selection or engineering of organic contact materials to minimize S, rather than empirical screening of candidate contacts.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is posed as an open research challenge in the photovoltaics community. Subsequent literature on perovskite/organic interfaces continues to investigate, but no widely accepted, fully predictive microscopic model of interface recombination yielding rational contact-design rules has been established; reviews up to 2024–2025 still describe contact selection as largely empirical and identify interface recombination understanding as an unresolved problem.

status_evidence.title: Minimizing non-radiative recombination losses in perovskite solar cells
status_evidence.snippet: Interface recombination remains the dominant loss channel in state-of-the-art perovskite solar cells, and a unified microscopic model linking molecular structure of organic transport layers to interfacial nonradiative rates is still lacking.
status_evidence.claim: Perovskite/organic interface recombination is acknowledged as not fully understood and contact optimization remains largely empirical.
